narrative.summary: Canada has no federal AI statute: the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act in Bill C-27 died when Parliament was prorogued on 6 January 2025, and a new privacy bill with a right to an explanation of automated decisions (C-36) and an online-safety bill covering chatbots and AI labelling (C-34) were at second reading in October 2026. Binding federal rules on AI are narrow: a 2026 Criminal Code offence for AI-generated intimate images, a 2026 election offence for fake images and voice imitations, and automated-decision powers in immigration and citizenship law, alongside PIPEDA and the Privacy Act. Federal policy rests on ISED's national AI strategy AI for All (June 2026), the Voluntary Code of Conduct on advanced generative AI (2023), the Canadian AI Safety Institute, and the Treasury Board's Directive on Automated Decision-Making with its Algorithmic Impact Assessment, generative AI guide, public-service AI strategy and AI register. Regulators add guidance and enforcement: the Privacy Commissioner's generative AI principles and findings on OpenAI, xAI, Clearview AI and TikTok, OSFI's model risk guideline E-23 (effective May 2027), Competition Bureau work on AI and algorithmic pricing, Health Canada's machine-learning medical device guidance, the Cyber Centre's AI security guidance and a CRTC broadcasting policy on human creative roles. Quebec's Law 25 gives rights over automated decisions and the province regulates public-sector AI by ministerial order; Ontario's Bill 194 and AI directive govern public-sector AI and its job-posting rule requires AI disclosure, Manitoba passed two AI Acts in 2026, and Toronto, Montréal and Québec City have their own AI policies.

Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
Ministère de la Cybersécurité et du Numérique (Quebec) and Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec
narrative.review_notes: Deep review completed on 11 October 2026, covering federal laws and bills, federal departments and the AI Safety Institute, federal regulators, all provinces and territories (in most depth Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta), and the cities of Toronto, Montréal, Québec City, Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Edmonton. Searches were made in English and French. Some official websites could not be read automatically, including the CRTC's decision pages, the Autorité des marchés financiers, Ontario's privacy commissioner, Montréal's document system and some canada.ca pages; records from those sites are marked as located but not fully read, or held as pending. Bills that died in 2025 or are still before Parliament, including Bill C-27 and its AI act, are listed as pending rather than as instruments. Pending: Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Edmonton staff AI rules, which were not found on official city sites; AI guidance in Saskatchewan, Yukon, the Northwest Territories and New Brunswick; regulations under Ontario's Bill 194; and the national adoption of ISO/IEC 42001.

instruments.official_title: Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All
instruments.english_title: Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All
instruments.issuing_authority: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation); launched by the Prime Minister
instruments.publisher_name: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
instruments.current_status: Launched 4 June 2026 (Prime Minister's news release of that date; ISED page date-modified 2026-06-08). The 50-page PDF (catalogue Iu4-458/2026E-PDF, ISBN 978-0-662-35657-8, © Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry 2026) was read in full; French version: « Stratégie nationale du Canada en matière d'intelligence artificielle : L'IA pour tous ». The title 'AI for All' is official. A strategy, not law: the legislative measures it announces (privacy, online safety) are separate bills. Followed the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy (2017) and the October 2025 national consultation.
instruments.summary: Canada's renewed national AI strategy, launched by Prime Minister Carney on 4 June 2026, organised around three principles (trust, opportunity, sovereignty) and six pillars: protecting Canadians and safeguarding democracy, empowering Canadians, powering AI adoption, building a sovereign AI foundation, scaling Canadian champions and building trusted international partnerships. It commits to modernised privacy and online-safety laws, AI transparency work (including watermarking), $50 million to expand the Canadian AI Safety Institute, a Canada Trusted AI Certification program and renewed funding for the Standards Council of Canada's AI program. Targets include raising business AI adoption from 12% to 60% by 2034, free AI literacy training, a public AI supercomputer and an AI Missions Program starting with health.

French: Stratégie en matière d'IA pour la fonction publique fédérale 2025-2027.
instruments.summary: Canada's first AI strategy for the federal public service, covering organisations subject to the Policy on Service and Digital, with four priority areas: central AI capacity (an AI Centre of Expertise, shared infrastructure and approved models), policy, legislation and governance (common AI lifecycle frameworks and an AI ethics review), talent and training, and engagement, transparency and value to Canadians. Commitments include departments identifying three high-potential AI areas, a public AI register and lighthouse projects such as GCtranslate, with renewal in 2027.

instruments.official_title: Direction on Government of Canada Cyber Security Readiness in the Frontier Artificial Intelligence Era: Security Policy Implementation Notice (SPIN)
instruments.english_title: Direction on Government of Canada Cyber Security Readiness in the Frontier AI Era (SPIN)
instruments.issuing_authority: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat
instruments.current_status: Effective 1 October 2026 (as stated in the notice). Issued as 'Direction'; it states that it does not replace existing obligations. Not a standalone Treasury Board policy; SPINs implement the Policy on Government Security.
instruments.summary: Security Policy Implementation Notice directing organisations subject to the Policy on Government Security to raise cyber readiness against frontier-AI-enabled threats, reinforcing the Policy on Government Security, the Policy on Service and Digital and the Directive on Security Management. Departments are to identify and prioritise critical services (list due in TBS's EPM tool by 30 November 2026), accelerate alert triage and risk-based patching and use defensive AI responsibly, harden identity and privileged access, fortify edge devices and networks, monitor with central logging and EDR/XDR, and prepare incident response and tested backups.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Canadian federal instrument shaping AI governance (cyber-security, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: Careful adoption of agentic AI
instruments.english_title: Careful adoption of agentic AI
instruments.issuing_authority: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, jointly with ASD's ACSC, CISA, NSA, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK
instruments.current_status: Released 1 May 2026 (Cyber Centre news item 'Joint guidance on the careful adoption of agentic artificial intelligence services', date modified 2026-05-01; same-day CISA release). Full text hosted on cyber.gc.ca (page date modified 2026-09-10).
instruments.summary: Joint Five Eyes guidance on securing LLM-based agentic AI systems used by government, critical infrastructure and industry. It explains agentic AI and how it differs from generative AI, sets out privilege, design and configuration, behavioural, structural and accountability risks, and recommends best practices such as aligning agentic AI with existing security models, adopting it cautiously and never granting broad or unrestricted access.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Canadian federal instrument shaping AI governance (cyber-security, generative-ai).

instruments.current_status: Dated May 2026 (Awareness series); page date modified 2026-05-29.

It adds a section on frontier AI, recommending AI-native defences and human oversight of high-impact decisions.

instruments.english_title: Principles for responsible, trustworthy and privacy-protective generative AI technologies (joint statement of federal, provincial and territorial privacy commissioners)
instruments.issuing_authority: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, jointly with the provincial and territorial information and privacy commissioners and ombuds
instruments.publisher_name: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
instruments.current_status: Not binding on specific investigations; the text notes many of its 'should' considerations are legal requirements under applicable privacy law. French title: Principes pour des technologies de l'IA générative responsables, dignes de confiance et respectueuses de la vie privée. Publication date source (date audit 2026-10-13): OPC page, date under the title: 'December 7, 2023' (separate 'Date modified: 2025-05-06' ignored).
instruments.summary: Sets out how key Canadian privacy principles apply to generative AI, with considerations for developers and providers of foundation models and generative AI systems and for organizations using them: legal authority and consent, appropriate purposes, necessity and proportionality, openness, accountability, individual access, data minimization, accuracy and safeguards. It anticipates 'no-go zones' such as creating AI content, including deepfakes, for malicious purposes (e.g. bypassing authentication or generating intimate images of identifiable people without consent) and asks developers, providers and users to give particular consideration to risks for vulnerable groups.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Canadian federal regulator instrument shaping AI governance (generative-ai, data-privacy).

instruments.official_title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
instruments.english_title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (S.C. 2000, c. 5) — PIPEDA
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: S.C. 2000, c. 5, assented to 13 April 2000. Per the note to s.72 in the consolidation, Parts 2-4 came into force on 1 May 2000, Part 1 (protection of personal information in the private sector) on 1 January 2001 (SI/2000-29) and Part 5 on 1 June 2009. Consolidation current to 2026-09-21, last amended 2025-03-04 (2024, c. 17). Amendments not in force: Division 23 of the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, ss.389-397, assented 26 March 2026) adds Division 1.2 'Mobility of Personal Information' (data mobility frameworks, s.10.4-10.6) on a day to be fixed by order. The Act contains no provision that mentions artificial intelligence or automated decisions; it is recorded as the general private-sector privacy law governing personal data used to train and deploy AI. Bill C-27 (44th Parliament), which would have replaced Part 1 with the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, died on the Order Paper on 6 January 2025; Bill C-36 (45th Parliament, first reading 15 June 2026) would again repeal Part 1 and enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act (see leads). French title: Loi sur la protection des renseignements personnels et les documents électroniques.
instruments.summary: Canada's federal private-sector privacy law. Part 1 governs the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by organizations in the course of commercial activities (and by federal works, undertakings or businesses about their employees), requiring knowledge and consent and compliance with the ten fair-information principles of the CSA Model Code set out in Schedule 1 (accountability, identifying purposes, consent, limiting collection, limiting use/disclosure/retention, accuracy, safeguards, openness, individual access, challenging compliance). It requires reporting of breaches of security safeguards posing a real risk of significant harm (Division 1.1) and lets individuals complain to the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, who investigates, may audit and enter compliance agreements, with recourse to the Federal Court; Part 2 governs electronic documents and signatures.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: General private-sector privacy law; governs personal information used to develop, train and deploy AI systems in commercial activity (no AI-specific provisions).

instruments.official_title: Privacy Act
instruments.english_title: Privacy Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. P-21)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: Consolidated as R.S.C., 1985, c. P-21 (originally enacted as Schedule II to S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 111). The consolidation does not state the original commencement date; the Government of Canada (Department of Finance ATIP page) states that the Privacy Act came into force on 1 July 1983. Consolidation current to 2026-09-21, last amended 2025-06-02 (2024, c. 20). The Act contains no provision that mentions artificial intelligence or automated decision-making; it is recorded as the federal public-sector privacy law that governs personal information used by government institutions, including in automated decision systems (Treasury Board's Directive on Automated Decision-Making operates alongside it). French title: Loi sur la protection des renseignements personnels.
instruments.summary: Federal public-sector privacy law governing how government institutions listed in the Schedule collect, use, disclose, retain and dispose of personal information. Institutions may collect personal information only if it relates directly to an operating program or activity (s.4), must use it only for the purpose collected or a consistent use (s.7) and disclose it only as permitted by s.8, and must describe their holdings in personal information banks; individuals have a right of access to and correction of their personal information (ss.12-17). The Privacy Commissioner of Canada investigates complaints and reviews compliance, with review by the Federal Court for refused access.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Governs personal information that federal institutions use in AI and automated decision systems; complements the Treasury Board Directive on Automated Decision-Making.
metadata_gaps: publication_date: only the consolidation year (R.S.C., 1985) is stated on the official page

instruments.official_title: Protecting Victims Act
instruments.english_title: Protecting Victims Act (S.C. 2026, c. 19; Bill C-16, 45th Parliament)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: Bill C-16 (45th Parliament, 1st session): first reading 9 December 2025, passed the House 11 June 2026 and the Senate 18 June 2026; royal assent 18 June 2026 (S.C. 2026, c. 19). Under s.205(1) the provisions, including s.15 (Criminal Code s.162.1), come into force on the 30th day after royal assent, i.e. 18 July 2026; some other provisions await a later date or order (s.205(2)-(4)). The consolidated Criminal Code s.162.1 now carries the amended definition (history '2014, c. 31, s. 3; 2026, c. 19, s. 15'). French title: Loi visant à protéger les victimes.
instruments.summary: Omnibus criminal-law Act whose s.15 amends the Criminal Code offence of publishing or distributing intimate images without consent (s.162.1) so that 'intimate image' also covers a visual representation made by any electronic or mechanical means, 'including by means of artificial intelligence software', that shows an identifiable person nude or engaged in explicit sexual activity and is likely to be mistaken for a real recording. It also adds a new offence of threatening to publish an intimate image (s.162.1(1.1)), punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment on indictment. Other parts create a coercive-control offence, make femicide first-degree murder in listed circumstances and change criminal procedure and corrections law.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Criminalizes non-consensual distribution of AI-generated sexual deepfakes of identifiable persons (Criminal Code s.162.1(2)(b)).

instruments.official_title: Strong and Free Elections Act
instruments.english_title: Strong and Free Elections Act (S.C. 2026, c. 20; Bill C-25, 45th Parliament)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: Bill C-25 (45th Parliament, 1st session): first reading 26 March 2026, passed the House 11 June 2026 and the Senate 18 June 2026; royal assent 18 June 2026 (S.C. 2026, c. 20). The only commencement provision (s.89) defers ss.88-88.2 (electoral district names) to the 90th day after assent; the Canada Elections Act consolidation lists amendments by 2026, c. 20 in force on 2026-06-18 and 2026-09-16, and the consolidated s.480.1 carries the new text (history '2014, c. 12, s. 88; 2018, c. 31, s. 322; 2026, c. 20, s. 48'). The Act does not use the words 'artificial intelligence' or 'deepfake'; it targets fabricated images, voice imitations and audio recordings by any means. French title: Loi sur des élections fortes et libres.
instruments.summary: Amends the Canada Elections Act on foreign influence, misleading information, contributions, party privacy policies and enforcement. Its s.48 replaces the impersonation offence (s.480.1) so that it is an offence, with intent to mislead, to create or distribute an image likely to be mistaken for an image of, or an imitation of the voice or an audio recording falsely representing anything said by, the Chief Electoral Officer, election officers, party leaders, candidates, potential, prospective, nomination and leadership contestants and others listed, with an exception for manifest parody or satire. It also requires registered and eligible parties to file a policy for the protection of personal information with the Chief Electoral Officer.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Prohibits synthetic image and voice impersonation (deepfakes) of electoral officials, parties and candidates (Canada Elections Act s.480.1(1)(c)-(e)).

instruments.official_title: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
instruments.english_title: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (S.C. 2001, c. 27)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: S.C. 2001, c. 27, assented to 1 November 2001; most provisions in force 28 June 2002 (SI/2002-97). Section 186.1 (Electronic Administration) was added by s.175 of the Economic Action Plan 2015 Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2015, c. 36, Division 15 of Part 3), which came into force on a day fixed by order in council (s.176(2)); the consolidation does not state that date, but s.186.1 appears in force (unshaded) in the consolidation current to 2026-09-21 (Act last amended 2026-03-26). Parallel 'for greater certainty' automated-system clauses exist in the Citizenship Act s.28.2(4) (added by S.C. 2023, c. 26, s.305) and the Pilotage Act s.46.01(4) (S.C. 2019, c. 29, s.251). French title: Loi sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés.
instruments.summary: Canada's immigration and refugee statute. Section 186.1 authorizes the Minister to administer and enforce the Act by electronic means and provides (s.186.1(5)) that 'an electronic system, including an automated system,' may be used by the Minister to make a decision or determination under the Act, or by an officer to make a decision or determination or proceed with an examination, if the Minister makes the system available. It is the statutory basis for automated and analytics-assisted triage and decision-making in immigration processing by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada and the Canada Border Services Agency.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Express statutory authority for automated decision-making in immigration decisions (s.186.1(5)).

instruments.official_title: Citizenship Act
instruments.english_title: Citizenship Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-29)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Canada
instruments.publisher_name: Department of Justice Canada (Justice Laws Website)
instruments.current_status: Consolidated as R.S.C., 1985, c. C-29; current to 2026-09-21, last amended 2025-12-15. Part VI.1 (Electronic Administration and Enforcement, ss.28.2-28.4) was added by s.305 of the Budget Implementation Act, 2023, No. 1 (S.C. 2023, c. 26, assented 22 June 2023) and appears in force in the consolidation; the commencement date of s.305 is not stated in the consolidation. The commencement date of the Act itself is not stated on the official page. French title: Loi sur la citoyenneté.
instruments.summary: Federal citizenship statute. Part VI.1 lets the Minister administer and enforce the Act by electronic means and provides (s.28.2(4)) that 'an electronic system, including an automated system, may be used to process an application, proceed with an examination or make a decision or determination under this Act'; s.28.3 treats electronic versions of signatures, applications, decisions and notices as meeting the Act's requirements. It is the statutory basis for automated processing of citizenship applications.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Express statutory authority for automated decision-making on citizenship applications (s.28.2(4)).

instruments.english_title: Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy

instruments.official_title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems
instruments.english_title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems
instruments.issuing_authority: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry)
instruments.publisher_name: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
instruments.current_status: Announced and effective immediately on 27 September 2023 (ISED news release, Montréal). The ISED page (dated 'September 2023', date modified 2026-06-04) lists 46 signatories as of October 2026, including Ada, Amii, BlackBerry, CGI, CIBC, Cohere, IBM, Mastercard, Mila, OpenText, Salesforce, TELUS and the Vector Institute. Originally described as a bridge to the proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Bill C-27), which died on the Order Paper in January 2025; the code remains published. Supported by an Implementation guide for managers of AI systems and an FAQ.
instruments.summary: Voluntary commitments for organisations that develop or manage the operations of advanced generative AI systems with general-purpose capabilities, structured around six outcomes: accountability, safety, fairness and equity, transparency, human oversight and monitoring, and validity and robustness. A measures table sets which measures apply to developers and managers of all advanced generative systems and which apply additionally to systems available for public use (e.g. third-party audits before release, watermarking/detection of AI-generated content, adversarial testing). It does not change existing legal obligations such as PIPEDA; signatories commit to apply it.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Canadian federal instrument shaping AI governance (generative-ai, ethics, risk-assurance).

instruments.summary: Federal Court policy on its own use of AI by judges, associate judges and law clerks, committing that the Court will not use AI, and in particular automated decision-making tools, to make its judgments and orders without first holding public consultations. It sets principles of accountability, respect for judicial independence and fundamental rights, non-discrimination, accuracy using certified or verified sources, cybersecurity and privacy, and human verification of AI outputs ('human in the loop'). It also records that AI tools assist language specialists in translating Federal Court decisions, under quality control by the Courts Administration Service.

instruments.summary: Advisory guidelines for Canadian courts and judges, drafted by the Council's Technology Committee, built on the premise that judges may not delegate decision-making to AI. Seven guidelines ask courts to protect judicial independence, use AI consistently with core values and ethical rules, have regard to the legal aspects of AI use, subject AI tools to stringent information security standards and output safeguards, use only AI tools able to give understandable explanations of their output, regularly track the impact of AI deployments, and provide education and user support.

instruments.english_title: Practice notice: Use of artificial intelligence in IRB proceedings
instruments.issuing_authority: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Chairperson)
instruments.publisher_name: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada
instruments.current_status: Signed on 10 July 2026 by Chairperson Manon Brassard; in effect from 7 September 2026. The IRB news item states that Board staff's own AI use is governed by internal policies and directives that prohibit using AI when preparing and deciding cases (not published). Publication date source: 'Signed on July 10, 2026' in the notice.
instruments.summary: Practice notice for all parties and counsel in all four IRB divisions, making parties accountable for the accuracy of AI-generated content, including verification of legal principles and citations, and warning against padding submissions or exposing sensitive information to AI tools. It prohibits using AI to generate or materially change content that reports a person's evidence, such as basis of claim narratives, affidavits, witness statements, photographs or videos, and requires a declaration when AI is used to generate or materially change content in documents submitted to the IRB. If the notice is not followed, the IRB may refuse or decline to rely on a document, draw negative inferences about credibility, report counsel to their regulator or restrict counsel from appearing.

instruments.summary: Shared values to guide federal, provincial and territorial governments in the responsible and ethical adoption and use of AI across Canada's health systems. Nine principles cover person-centricity, equity, diversity and inclusion, privacy and security, safety and oversight across the AI lifecycle, accountability and responsibility of developers, purchasers, operators and regulators, transparency and understandability, AI literacy, robust data and data practices, and Indigenous-led governance and data sovereignty. Quebec shares some principles but keeps full autonomy over its health system.

Text read at https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/45-1/bill/C-36/first-reading: enacts the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, repeals Part 1 of PIPEDA (renamed the Electronic Documents Act), and Part 3 creates a Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada. It defines 'automated decision system' (rules-based systems, regression, predictive analytics, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks) and requires organizations to give a general account of their use of such systems for predictions, recommendations or decisions with legal or similarly significant effects and, on request, an explanation of such a prediction, recommendation or decision (type and source of personal information and principal reasons). Charter Statement tabled 19 August 2026. Record if enacted.
